name: Tiffany Blue
lede: Tiffany Blue is the pale, robin's-egg turquoise Tiffany & Co. has used since its 1837 "Blue Book" catalog, trademarked in 1998 and given its own custom Pantone number, 1837, for the year the company was founded.

sections.title: A color old enough to outlast three owners of the name
sections.body: The color first appears on the cover of Tiffany & Co.'s "Blue Book" catalog in 1837, the same year the company was founded [1]. Paterson's dictionary of color simply calls it the turquoise-blue color adopted by Tiffany, the jewelers, with no further history attached [2]. Tiffany & Co. trademarked the exact shade in 1998, and in 2001 worked with Pantone to standardize a custom color for the brand's own use, numbered 1837 after the founding year rather than given a name [1][3]. Westland's broader point about why any brand bothers locking down one exact color applies directly here: a small set of highly saturated, easily distinguished hues works far better than a subtle one for building a strong, clear identity, which is also why Coca-Cola's red is so tightly associated with soft drinks generally [1]. Eckstut makes the sharper, color-specific version of the same point: most people could not name ten blues if asked, but having once seen a Tiffany box, this particular blue becomes instantly recognizable the moment the name "Tiffany blue" is said aloud — naming and repetition, not the hue alone, do the real work [3]. Our own hex value here is necessarily approximate: this is a trademarked brand color kept as a manual addition to the library rather than a color any public dictionary measured and filed, and no real 1955 ISCC-NBS filing exists for a brand name that postdates that system by decades [4].

sections.title: Its neighbors, and a crowded family of aliases
sections.body: In the color graph, Tiffany Blue sits 2.5 units from [[light-sea-green]], almost the same color, and 2.7 units from [[maximum-blue-green]], also almost indistinguishable [5]. [[keppel]], 5.8 units off, is greener; [[dark-turquoise]], 6.0 off, is lighter; [[tyrolite-green]] and [[blue-turquoise]], both 6.0 off, are duller [5]. Beyond those, cross-system name lists file an identical or near-identical color under more than a dozen other names, among them Topaz, Lapis, Bewitch and Bright Jade Green — a sign of how many separate naming traditions, jewelry trade names among them, converge independently on roughly this same pale aqua, long before or entirely apart from any jeweler's marketing department [5].

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Fittingly for a jeweler's color, its two nearest gem twins are Tourmaline, 5.5 units off, and Garnet, 8.0 off [6]. Pantone has returned to close relatives of this color twice as its own Color of the Year: Turquoise in 2010, 3.4 units from Tiffany Blue, and Blue Turquoise in 2005, 4.8 off [7]. Among design aesthetics, the closest full-palette match is Memphis design, 1.7 units off on its neighbor Verdigris, with Seapunk and Corporate Memphis further out at 4.2 and 4.9 units [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,778-painting archive carries this color covering even 1 percent of its canvas, as photographed [9]. That is itself the honest finding, not a gap in the data: almost every painting in the archive predates 1998, the year the trademark locked this exact shade down, and most predate 1837 as well, so there is no reason to expect a match [9]. A handful of our look-alike neighbors, Light Sea Green and Maximum Blue Green among them, are old enough and common enough that a reader curious what a bluish-green of this general character looks like on a real canvas can follow those links instead [9]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test, and a true zero is as real a result as any other number this method produces.

questions.q: In what year did Tiffany & Co. first use this color, on the cover of its "Blue Book" catalog?
Why does our painting archive find zero matches for Tiffany Blue?
choices: The color is a modern trademark that postdates almost every painting in the archive
Tiffany Blue does not actually exist as a real color
The archive only includes paintings from before 1837
questions.answer: The color is a modern trademark that postdates almost every painting in the archive

questions.q: What does Tiffany & Co.'s custom Pantone number, 1837, actually refer to?
choices: The year the company was founded
The exact wavelength of the color in nanometers
The number of jewelers who approved it
questions.answer: The year the company was founded

openers: Tiffany Blue's own Pantone number, 1837, is not a color code at all — it is the year the company was founded.
Our painting archive finds not one single match for Tiffany Blue, and that absence is itself the honest answer.

issues: Depth wave pilot: built from color-kb concordance (7 hits: Paterson, Westland, Eckstut) plus existing fact cards, the color graph's real look-alikes and cross-system aliases, and gem/look/fashion twins. The zero-presence archive result is reported as a genuine finding, not a gap, with the reason stated plainly.

Fresh-context fact-check (2026-10-09): every [n]-cited number checked against a freshly regenerated tools/depth_kit.py kit (la edges, real-vs-computed ISCC-NBS, archive fieldnotes, twins) and against CLAUDE.md's myth list. No issues found.
